title: Agents
text: Agents Crafting An agent is a frame that runs a program. Walking, carrying, reaping, mining and laying blocks are its own; where learning beats a rule, a model in one of its slots decides, in exactly the format of that model's test, and the agent does what the model answers. You can see a model in its lantern of a head, turning faster while it thinks. Home and models Where you place an agent is its home, and its work happens around home. Set home, the house beside its screen, makes where it stands its new home. It has two model slots, in the panel beside its screen. Its Model takes a Checkpoint with a model of up to 40,000 parameters, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server, for a model of any size: see Serving Models. This model writes the orders you give as programs, and makes the decisions of storing, hauling, building and copying. Its Filter takes a checkpoint that passes Sorting, and tells what kind each thing is. Its screen says what is missing. Programs The Program tab holds what it does when nothing else is asked of it: steps between commas, checked as you type. take bread, come, give bread until full (pickup) repeat (mine 4 stone, put) if ripe (harvest) else (wait 10) Run starts it and Stop stops it. A program that goes on for good, a repeat without a count, is its standing work; any other runs once, and then it rests. The buttons on the Work tab set ready-made programs: Farm is repeat (farm), Sort is repeat (sort), and so on, and Rest clears it. The Palette beside Stop lays out every piece of a program to click together instead of typing, each saying what it does when you point at it. Pieces go on the end, along with whatever plainly comes next: the ( that opens a block, the mark a place needs. To name a thing, pick it up and click the program, or the order box on the Work tab. The steps: come, home, go 3 to the third mark, stay, follow take 5 bread from the chests and barrels around home, put everything or put wheat away, give bread to you, fetch bread, which is taking, coming and giving pickup what lies around it, harvest, plant wheat seeds, till the grass near water, mine 4 stone (with a pickaxe it carries, for blocks that need one; it digs its way to anything buried, and to what a Surveyor found; mine caches for what the old world left in them; agents mining near each other take different blocks), place oak planks 2 on top of the second mark wait 10 seconds, say hello farm, store, sort, haul, build, copy or move: one round of a routine Blocks: repeat (…), repeat 3 (…), if … (…) else (…), until … (…) and wait until …. Checks: have 3 bread, stocked bread in the stores around home, ripe, full, night, near (you are within 8 blocks), powered 2 (the second mark has a redstone signal), each with not before it if need be. The trace The Trace tab shows what it did, checked and decided, newest last, and how each step went: storing and sorting note every stack they put away, and where. A step that fails says why, and the program goes on with the next. An agent that gets stuck on its way somewhere gives up after a while; stuck three times running, it jumps home. Routines farm: walks the farmland within 7 blocks of home, harvests what is ripe and plants what is bare, and takes the harvest to the chest at home, keeping some seed. It is a rule, so no model is asked. store: empties the barrels around home into the chests within 8 blocks, numbered 0 to 9, nearest first. A kind it has never seen goes to the emptiest chest. For a kind seen before, it shows its model where eight kinds went and asks which chest this one belongs in. sort: empties the barrels around home into the chests labelled with each thing's kind: Food, Plants, Wood, Stone, Ores or Tools. Name a chest in an anvil to label it, or fix a sign to it. Its filter is asked the kind of each thing by its name alone, so it can sort things it has never seen. Whatever its filter calls other, or is less than 60% sure of, goes in a chest labelled Other, or else in one with no label. haul: walks out along the six waymarks it was handed, loads up from the chest or barrel at the last one, and comes home. On the way back its model names the waymarks in reverse, and it walks wherever its model says. build, copy and move: carry on a pattern along a run, copy a build, or move it, contents and all, as its model reads it: see The Architect. The Survey Rod Crafting Use a Survey Rod on blocks to mark them, up to eight, in order; use a marked block again to unmark it, and sneak-use in the air to clear them all. Use the rod on an agent to hand it the marks: waymarks for hauling, a build's corners and where its copy goes, the ends of a run to build along, or places for go and place. Program Cards Crafting (Shapeless) A Program Card carries a program from agent to agent. Use a blank card on an agent to copy its program, and a written one to hand the program over; sneak-use a written card to copy onto it instead. In an agent's screen, click the program holding a written card to load what it says, or holding a blank card to write the program onto it; shift-click writes onto a written card too. Orders Start a chat message with an agent's name to give it an order: Pip, bring me some bread. It hears you within 24 blocks, or anywhere a Model Server's relays reach while you are in reach too, holding a Terminal tuned to it. You can also type an order on the Work tab of its screen and Tell it. Its model writes the order as a program. One step, or one of the jobs, it does at once. Anything else it reads back with [Do it] and [Cancel] to click in chat, or on the Work tab of its screen, and runs only once you say yes. An order comes before its program, which it goes back to after. If what its model writes is no program at all, it is puzzled; a model that never practised orders will mostly be puzzled.

title: The Architect
text: The Architect An agent whose model passes Induction can copy a build, move it, or carry on its pattern. It reads a build as slices across its length, a letter for each slice, and asks its model what comes next, just as the test does. Marks Mark blocks with a Survey Rod, in order, and hand the marks to the agent: copy and move: two blocks at opposite corners of the build, then the block the copy should stand on. The copy's first corner goes on top of the third mark, and the rest follows from there. build: the blocks under the two ends of a straight run. With a third mark on the far top corner of the first slice, each slice reaches across and up to it; without one, each slice is a single block. A build is cut across its longer side, into at most 16 slices, each at most 16 blocks wide and 16 high, and its copy stands within 64 blocks of it. Copying copy first reads the build. It shows its model the build's slices, a different letter for each, then the order it has read so far, and asks which slice comes next. The first slice it takes by itself, since nothing yet says where a copy begins. If its model is less than 60% sure, or names a slice twice, it stops before it lays anything. Then it lays each slice in its place, fetching the blocks from the chests and barrels around home, or from a storage network through a Storage Terminal there. Chests and machines in the copy start out empty. What can be built over, such as grass or water, isn't copied, and anything already standing where the copy goes stays. Until a block is laid, its place shows as a faint teal ghost to anyone nearby, for a copy, a move or a repeat alike. Moving move reads the build the same way and checks that nothing stands where the copy goes. Then it takes the build up slice by slice, contents and all, and lays it down again: chests keep their items and furnaces their fuel, and nothing drops on the way. Pictures and item frames are no blocks, and stay behind. An agent holding a build can't be picked up until it has laid it down. Repeating build carries on a pattern along its run. It shows its model the slices so far, the same letter for the same slice, and lays the slice its model names. Lay one round of the pattern and the start of the next by hand. What comes after a slice is what came after it last time, so the slices of one round must all differ.

title: The Archive
text: The Archive The old world wrote letters, journals, stories, songs, recipes, manuals and notices, and kept a copy of everything. What survives is in Archive Shards, each a piece of one record with some of its text lost. Shards A shard learns which record it is the first time you hold it. Use it to read what is left; lost text shows as ▒. Archive drives Crafting Use an Archive Drive to file every shard you carry into it. Shards of the same record make one better copy: whatever any of them kept is kept. The drive's tooltip counts its records and its legible letters. In a Model Core's Data slots, a drive is practice for Reading: the model learns to predict the next letter of everything legible on it, or the next token with a tokenizer, so the more you recover, the more it has to learn from. Reading is tested on records no shard ever carries. A model can only pass by learning how the old world wrote, not by remembering what it read. The Reader Crafting A Reader restores lost text. Put a shard in its tray and a model in its model slot: a checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server for a model too big to hold. The Reader goes through the lost blocks one by one. For each, the model reads the text just before the block and then guesses the block letter by letter, seeing each true letter after its guess. If it guesses at least half of them, the block was predictable enough to restore, and it comes back. A block the model cannot restore stays lost until a better model tries. A model that reads ahead, seeing the letter it is asked to guess, is turned away: it would only copy.

title: The Bench and the Fabricator
text: The Bench and the Fabricator Every machine is made in a Fabricator. The simple ones need nothing but materials. The rest need a Blank Photomask carrying a design for what they compute, and designs are wired on a Bench from the smallest operations there are. Crafting Crafting Crafting (Shapeless) Crafting (Shapeless) Specs The Bench lists specs: what a module must compute, a formula, and a set of test cases with the answers worked out exactly. Some cases are ordinary. Others are the inputs that break the obvious design: scores of a thousand, a row of equal numbers, numbers far from zero. A design passes when it gets every case right to within a thousandth. Specs build on each other. Attention needs your softmax and matrix multiply; the transformer block needs layer norm, attention and the feed-forward block. A spec opens when the ones it builds on are verified. Wiring a design Drag parts from the left onto the board, and drag from one node's right edge to another's left edge to wire them. Every node shows a strip of the numbers it computes on the chosen case; click it to read them. A strip turning red means a value that is not a number, and the node that turned it red is the one to look at. Wire your last node into result, and the cases on the right tell you which pass and why the others don't. The parts: Sources: a constant you type, and size, the length of the last axis. Arithmetic: add, sub, mul, div and max, element by element. An axis of size 1 stretches to match the other input, so a row of sums divides a whole row of numbers. Functions: neg, exp, log, sqrt and tanh. Last axis: sum and amax keep the axis with size 1; transpose swaps the last two axes; unsqueeze and squeeze add and drop an axis of size 1; causal hides everything above the diagonal. Your modules: every spec you have verified, as one part. Recording When every case passes, Record writes the design onto a blank photomask from your inventory, signed with your name. The spec counts as verified for you from then on, and its module joins your parts on every Bench. Fabricating Put a photomask in the Fabricator and pick a machine. Each takes a Tensor Casing, wafers, and weight crystals if it learns weights. A design's area sets the wafers: four units of area to a wafer. Each primitive costs a little area and each module what its spec's design costs, so a smaller design makes cheaper machines. The photomask is never used up. Without a mask, the Fabricator makes the machines that need no design: the embedding and position tables, the residual junction, the gate, the scaler, the causal mask, the head splitter and merger, the delay line and the concatenator. A matrix multiply photomask also makes the Training Accelerator, an attention photomask the Hourglass, and a transformer photomask Forecaster II and the Smelter. Fused and unfused The ruins hold old photomasks too, carrying salvaged designs: correct, but written out one primitive at a time. Machines made from them are unfused. They give the same answers, but they write out every tensor in between, so they use more memory and train more slowly. A design you verify yourself makes fused machines, one kernel each. The machine's screen and tooltip say which it is.

title: The Model Core
text: The Model Core The Model Core feeds text into your machines and judges what comes back. Its front sends out tokens; every other face takes in the model's scores. It trains the model, tests it, and saves it as a model. The trained weights stay in the machines themselves, so a model keeps what it learned when you leave and come back. Crafting Data Four slots for what the model practises on: datasets, archive drives, or a salvaged model. Everything in them is practised together, a batch from each in turn. Beside them are the tokenizer slot, for the tokens the model reads and writes, and the checkpoint slot. An empty slot shows faintly what goes in it; point at a checkpoint for what it holds. Save to checkpoint tests the model on every benchmark and saves it into that checkpoint. With a salvaged model loaded, Rebuild builds its machines in front of the Core: see Salvaged Models. Train The learning curve, with the numbers it ends at beneath it: train loss, test loss and accuracy. Point at them for Parameters, the model's weights, Grad norm, the size of the last gradient, and Threads, how many threads the Core trains with. Train starts training and stops it. Beside the window, a toolbar holds Reset and Check, then the settings: Speed, Learning rate, Batch and Clip. Point at one for its value and what it does; click for the next value, right-click for the one before. See Training for what each one means. Tests Every benchmark on a line, with its score at the last test; a full green bar passes. The test of each benchmark is taken while the model trains on it; Test all runs every test now. Point at a line for the job it is used for, the score that passes, when it was tested and the format its test uses. See Models and Tests. Try Runs the model. Choose a benchmark: Example draws a fresh test example and shows the model answering it, the way an agent would ask. For Orders, type an order and Ask; for Reading, type the start of something and Write: the model carries it on one letter at a time, drawing each from its predicted probabilities. Temp (temperature) sharpens or flattens those probabilities before drawing: Low temperatures repeat the model's favourite continuations; high ones take more risks. The bars show how likely the model found each candidate for the first letter it wrote. Inspect Every machine of the model in the order data reaches it, with its output shape, its number of weights and the size of its last gradient. Problems found by Check are listed here too. A bar that shrinks to nothing as you go down the list is a gradient that never arrives. More threads Each Training Accelerator touching the Core, directly or through other Accelerators, lends it one more thread, up to the limit the server allows. An Accelerator with nothing to cool it runs hot and lends half: give it water, ice or snow to touch. The Fabricator makes them from a matrix multiply photomask.

title: Serving Models
text: Serving Models A model too big for an agent's head can still work for it. A Model Server holds the model and answers questions for everything tuned to it, as far as its relays reach. The Model Server Crafting (Shapeless) Use a saved Checkpoint on a Model Server to load its model; sneak-use the server with an empty hand to take the checkpoint back. Use it to see what it is doing: the model it serves, how many answers a second it can give, how many questions are waiting and how many it has answered. A server gives 4 answers a second on its own. Each Training Accelerator touching it adds as many again, or half as many while it runs hot. Its front lights blink while it answers. When more than 64 questions wait, new ones are turned away until it catches up. Relays Crafting (Shapeless) A Model Server reaches 16 blocks by itself. A Relay within 32 blocks of the server, or of another relay already linked to it, links up and carries the server's reach 32 blocks around itself. Use a relay to see how many other relays are in reach and which servers it is linked to. Relay Cards Crafting (Shapeless) Use a Relay Card on a Model Server to tune it. In an agent's or a Reader's model slot, the card asks the server instead of carrying a model: any size of model, wherever the server's network reaches. Every agent tuned to one server shares its answers per second. The Terminal Crafting (Shapeless) Tune a Terminal on a Model Server the same way, then use it to talk to the served model: write the start of something and the model carries it on. While you hold a tuned Terminal within the server's reach, every agent the server reaches hears the orders you give by name in chat. Heat Accelerators run hot. One touching water, ice or snow, or standing in a cold biome, lends a full thread to a Core or a full share of answers to a server; one with nothing to cool it lends half, and smokes while it works.

title: Flight
text: Flight The Flight Frame is worn in the chest slot. While it has power and a pilot it can carry, a model that passes Pilot, its wearer flies as freely as in creative play: jump twice to take off, and it hovers wherever you stop. It spends 80 FE a tick while you fly, so a full frame of 400,000 FE flies for about four minutes. The Fabricator makes it from a transformer photomask. The pilot A pilot goes in as an item goes into a bundle: in your inventory, pick up a checkpoint and right-click the frame with it. Right-click the frame with nothing in hand to take the pilot out again, back on its checkpoint. The frame's tooltip names its pilot, and says when it cannot hold the frame: a pilot has to pass Pilot, and be small enough to carry. Power Use the frame on an Energy Cell to fill it from the cell's charge. The bar on the frame shows how much it holds. Learning to fly A model learns to pilot on the Flight Dataset, by flying: the Core flies the model's own flights and it learns from how each choice turned out, as for Control. Thrust changes how fast the frame climbs or sinks, not where it is, so a pilot has to read its speed from the heights before; and the wind its vane reads pushes every two or three looks from a moment of its own, which it has to make out from the flight and meet before it pushes. A model that sees only the last few characters holds under half of the flights in its worst wind; a two-block transformer holds them all after about a thousand steps. See Models and Tests.

title: The Forecaster
text: The Forecaster The Forecaster watches the blocks around it that make progress and writes down what they do: furnaces, smokers, blast furnaces, brewing stands, Fabricators, crops and the stems of pumpkins and melons. Give it a model that has learned what such blocks do next, and if the model's forecasts match what happened, it runs them ahead: it draws their next looks from the model and makes them so. Crafting Watching It watches everything within four blocks of it, on its own level or one above or below, and writes a line for each block. Machines. It looks at each furnace, smoker, blast furnace, brewing stand and Fabricator eight times an item, and writes down how far through its item it is: a when it has just begun, up to h at seven eighths. A furnace at work writes abcdefghabcdefghabcdefgh and a line ends once its machine has been seen idle twice: aa. A smoker cooks twice as fast as a furnace and is looked at twice as often, so its line reads the same, give or take a letter. A furnace that runs out of fuel halfway through an item cools back down, two ticks for every tick, and its line steps back: abcdefdbaa. Crops. Every twenty seconds it looks at every crop: wheat, carrots, potatoes, the stems of pumpkins and melons, and any crop that grows through the same seven ages. A crop's line is its age at every look, from 0 when planted to 7 when ripe, ending once it has been seen ripe twice. 00000011111111122222223333333334444445555555666666677 Only what a block did by itself counts. A crop that is harvested, trampled or fed bone meal starts a new line, so its lines only ever hold what the field really does. Put a Field Log in the Log slot to keep a copy. Crafting (Shapeless) A model of the blocks A model that has learned what happens next is a model of its world, and the Forecaster asks for nothing more. Train one on Forecasting at a Model Core: the Forecast Dataset holds the lines of many fields and machines. Crafting (Shapeless) A machine keeps its pace. Given where it is now, its next look is all but settled, so a model of machines in general forecasts yours. Crops are another matter. How fast a crop grows depends on its field: wet farmland or dry, in tidy rows or crowded. A model that learned from many fields expects the growth of an average one. That is close enough on some fields and far off on others. To forecast your own field, train on it. Put the Forecaster's Field Log in a data slot of the Core, on its own, and the model learns this field's pace. It gets worse at fields in general, and may even fail the Forecasting test: that is the price of fitting one field well. Beside the Forecast Dataset, the log only pulls the model halfway. Calibration A forecast is only worth acting on if it is right on average. The Forecaster checks a model against everything it watched, lines still being written included: the crops that finish first are the ones that happened to grow fastest, so finished lines alone would flatter a model that expects too much. It checks crops and machines apart, once the crops have grown 100 ages by themselves, or the machines have made 100 eighths of items, about a dozen, at their own pace. At every look it adds up how far the model expected the block to move, and divides by how far it moved: Within 11% of 1, it runs those blocks four looks for every one. Within 25%, two. Further off, it refuses the model for them. The screen shows the blocks nearby from above, then how far they moved per look from each age or each eighth, for the kind picked with the tabs: amber for what the blocks did, teal for what the model expected. A model that expects too much from young crops, or too little from old ones, shows it there. Below, a row for each kind shows the progress seen so far, then how close the model came and how fast it runs them. A refused model is checked again each time those blocks have moved 25 more, and any model is checked again when it changes. Running ahead At every look, each growing crop's line goes to the model, which draws the crop's next look from its probabilities, then the next, as many as the model has earned. The crop grows to the age drawn. At every look at a machine, its line goes to the model the same way, and the machine works through the progress the model drew, a few ticks at a time: a furnace run four looks for every one cooks four items in the time of one, on the same fuel per item. Every look drawn is the model's own work. A model that is slow to answer, or a server busy with other askers, runs fewer looks ahead. Lines the model wrote, or that a machine was run ahead through, are never written down: the log only ever holds what the blocks did by themselves. Forecaster II Forecaster II watches and checks the same way, and runs blocks further ahead when its model comes closer: within 5% of what they did, eight looks for every one, and within 2.5%, sixteen. Every look it runs ahead is one more the model draws, so a block at ×16 asks fifteen of the model for each look the world takes; a slow model, or a busy server, runs fewer. The Fabricator makes it from a transformer photomask. A model of machines in general expects a run of items to end now and then, so it falls a few percent short of furnaces that never run out. One that has also learned from this Forecaster's own log knows better. The Hourglass The Hourglass keeps time while you carry it, a second for every second, up to an hour. The Fabricator makes it from an attention photomask, out of a Tensor Casing, four wafers and two weight crystals. Sneak-use a Forecaster to bind it. Then use it on a machine or a crop of a kind that Forecaster runs ahead, anywhere in the Forecaster's dimension while the Forecaster is loaded: the block runs twice as fast for thirty seconds. Use it on the block again before that ends and the pace doubles, for thirty seconds from then, up to sixteen times as fast. Each step costs twice the kept time of the one before: thirty seconds of it for twice as fast, four minutes for sixteen times. It works only on what its Forecaster's model is trusted with: while the model doesn't pass its check on machines, the Hourglass refuses machines too. A Forecaster never writes down the line of a block an Hourglass ran.

title: Getting Started
text: Getting Started A first model fits in a few blocks: a Model Core, an Embedding Table and some Signal Cable. It learns what the blocks around you do next. A Forecaster puts that to work: once its forecasts hold, your furnaces run four times as fast. Materials Tensor Casing is the shell of every machine; Weight Crystal holds learned numbers, so machines with weights need them. Crafting Crafting Then craft the Model Core, a stack of cables and a Forecast Dataset: endless lines of crops growing and machines at work, to learn from. Crafting Crafting Crafting (Shapeless) Machines are made in a Fabricator. With no photomask in it, it makes the Embedding Table from a casing, a Wafer and a weight crystal. Crafting Crafting (Shapeless) Build it Place the Model Core. Its front turns toward you: tokens come out of it. Lay a cable from the Core's front to a free spot a few blocks away. Place the Embedding Table against the end of that cable. It snaps into the flow: its back reads the cable and its front points away. Lay a cable from the table's front back to any other face of the Core: its sides, its top or its back. That is where the model's scores go in. Open the table and set Width to V (vocab). The two cables never touch, so they form two separate networks: one carries tokens to the table, the other carries the table's scores back. Train it Open the Core and put the Forecast Dataset in one of its Data slots. Switch to Train and press Train. Two curves fall: the loss on practice, and the loss on the test, which only uses lines the model never practised on. Each line in the dataset is one block, looked at again and again. A furnace's line is how far it is through the item it is making, from a just begun to h nearly done, then round again: abcdefghabcdefgh. A crop's line is its age at every look, from 0 to 7. An Embedding Table set to V scores the next look from the one before it, and for a machine the look before all but settles the next. When Forecasting on the Tests tab gets below 0.21, the model is ready. Save it Craft a Checkpoint, put it in the Core's checkpoint slot and press Save to checkpoint. The Core tests the model on every benchmark and keeps it, scores and all, in the crystal. The machines can go on training; the checkpoint keeps this moment. Crafting Run your furnaces ahead Craft a Forecaster and place it among your furnaces, smokers or blast furnaces: within four blocks, on its own level or one above or below. Put the checkpoint in its Model slot, and keep the furnaces fed and fuelled. Crafting The Forecaster looks at each machine eight times an item and writes down how far it got. Once the machines have made about a dozen items at their own pace, it checks the model against what they did. If the progress the model expects is within 11% of the progress there was, it runs them four looks for every one: the model draws each machine's next looks, and the machine works through them. Within 25%, two. The Forecaster tells the rest, crops included. Further Better models need machines built from designs: wire them yourself on a Bench, or go looking for the old ones in the ruins. Storage keeps what your furnaces make: a Port under each one carries it onto drives, and a Storage Terminal finds it again. Agents run programs you click together: they mine, carry, build and sort, and models fill in where learning beats a rule. Look at any machine to see its name, its output shape (or what is wrong with it) and what the face you are looking at does. Sneak-use a machine's face to point its output there. Training runs on its own threads. Place Training Accelerator blocks against the Core to give it more, and keep them cool.

title: Residual
text: Residual Someone lived here before you. They seem to have built machines that thought, and they wrote everything down. Then they were gone. Pieces of what they left still turn up in the ruins: broken tablets of their writing, the designs of their machines, and models that no longer work. These are field notes on building models again: language models made of machines that each do one operation, cabled into a network, trained on text, and tested on text they have never seen. A model that knows what the blocks around it will do next lets a Forecaster run them ahead of time. Others carry on a pattern, tell what a thing is by its name, turn what you say into programs for agents, and read what the old world wrote. Start here Getting Started: a first model, and furnaces that run four times as fast. The Bench and the Fabricator: machines wired from the smallest operations there are. Ruins: where the old world's things are. Milestones: every advancement, lit once you have made it, and how to make the rest. Models The Archive: shards, drives, and restoring what was lost. The Bench and the Fabricator: designs wired from primitives, and the machines made from them. The Model Core: where models are built, trained, tested and saved. Tokens: the BPE Forge, and vocabularies learned from the archive. Training: reading a loss curve, and the settings that shape it. Models and Tests: the ten benchmarks, checkpoints, and how big a model may be. Salvaged Models: broken models from the ruins. Putting models to work The Forecaster: a model of the blocks around it, trusted only as far as it is right, runs them ahead. Agents: frames that run programs, with models where learning beats a rule. The Architect: agents that copy, move and repeat builds, read as letters a slice at a time. The Surveyor: a model that finds the ores in the ground around it, read a row at a time. Serving Models: Model Servers, relays and the Terminal. The base Storage: drives that keep any number of kinds, a terminal that finds anything, and Ports that move items between the network and every chest and machine, 1,280 a second. Power: generators, cables and cells, and a Smelter that makes two ingots from every ore, three with a controller. Flight: the flight frame, flown by a pilot you train. Reference Machines and Cables: how values travel between blocks. The Residual Stream: the running sum every transformer layer reads and adds to. Shapes: what [B×T×C] means, and how to fix a shape error. Machines, one page each.

title: Activation
text: Activation Bends every number through the same nonlinear function. Without one, two Linear Layers in a row multiply out into a single Linear Layer, however many you stack: the activation is what lets depth add anything. Shapes Any shape in, the same shape out. Settings Function: ReLU by default. ReLU keeps positive numbers and zeroes the rest. Its slope is 0 or 1, so it never shrinks a gradient that passes. GELU is a smooth ReLU, used by GPT-2 and BERT. SiLU is z·σ(z), used inside the feed-forward layers of LLaMA and its relatives. tanh squashes into (−1, 1), as in the first neural language models. sigmoid squashes into (0, 1). Its slope is at most a quarter, so every sigmoid layer shrinks the gradient that passes back through it. Parameters None. In PyTorch F.relu(x) F.gelu(x, approximate="tanh") F.silu(x) torch.tanh(x) torch.sigmoid(x) Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of GELU: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Residual Junction
text: Residual Junction Adds its two inputs, number by number. It has two jobs. It combines token and position vectors, and it makes residual connections: adding a branch's output back onto the stream that went into it, so the branch refines the stream instead of replacing it. Shapes Two equal shapes, or a smaller one that matches the end of the larger and repeats across it: [B×T×C] and [T×C] make [B×T×C]. Parameters None. In PyTorch x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x)) Notes The identity term in its gradient gives every layer a direct path back to the loss. That is why stacks of residual layers keep learning when plain stacks stall. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Attention Head
text: Attention Head Multi-head causal self-attention in one machine: the attention you can build from Linear Layers, a Matrix Multiplier, a Causal Mask and a Softmax, with queries, keys and values all computed from its one input, a causal mask built in, several heads and an output projection. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Heads: 1, 2, 4 or 8. 4 by default. The width C must divide evenly by it. Each head works on C/H of the numbers and scales its scores by 1/√(C/H). Parameters 4 × C²: the matrices W_Q, W_K, W_V and W_O, without biases. In PyTorch self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(C, heads=4) x = x + self.attn(self.norm1(x)) Notes After training, its picture shows where its first head looks: one row per position, one column for every position it can see. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Attention: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Causal Mask
text: Causal Mask Sets every score above the diagonal of a T × T grid to −∞. After a Softmax those become weights of exactly zero, so position t gives no weight to anything after t. Shapes A grid of scores […×T×T] in, the same shape out. Parameters None. In PyTorch def causal_mask(scores): T = scores.shape[-1] future = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), diagonal=1) return scores.masked_fill(future, float("-inf")) Notes It belongs between the scores and the Softmax. Without it, a model trained to predict the next token can simply read it, and its loss falls to almost nothing while it learns nothing. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Concatenator
text: Concatenator Joins two vectors end to end: the main input's numbers first, then the side input's. Shapes […×a] and […×b] in, […×(a + b)] out. Every size but the last must match. Parameters None. In PyTorch x = torch.cat([a, b], dim=-1) Notes A Linear Layer after a Concatenator computes the same thing as two Linear Layers, one on each input, added together. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Embedding Table
text: Embedding Table Looks up a learned row of numbers for each token: token i gets row i of a table with one row per vocabulary entry. This is how text enters a model, so the table must be fed directly by the Model Core's front. Shapes Tokens [B×T] in, [B×T×C] out, where C is the Width. Settings Width: V, or 4 to 256. 32 by default. At V, each row can serve directly as the scores for the next token: a bigram model. Parameters V × C, drawn from a normal distribution with spread 1. In PyTorch self.embed = nn.Embedding(V, C) e = self.embed(tokens) Notes After training, the weights picture shows the table, a row per token. Tokens that behave alike end up with similar rows, which is how what the model learns about one carries over to others. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Machines
text: Machines Each machine performs one operation of a model, with the same arithmetic as PyTorch. A machine takes its main input on its back and, if it has one, its side input on any other face, and sends its result out of its front: see Machines and Cables. Right-click a machine to change its settings and see what it computes. Every machine comes out of the Fabricator. The simple ones need no design; the rest need a photomask of the spec that describes them, verified on a Bench or salvaged from the ruins. No design needed Embedding Table: token ids to vectors. Position Table: a learned vector for every position. Residual Junction: addition, and with it the residual stream. Gate: one signal opening or closing another. Scaler: multiplied by a constant, usually 1/√d. Causal Mask: the future hidden. Head Splitter and Head Merger: multi-head attention from parts. Delay Line: a fixed look back in time. Concatenator: two vectors joined end to end. From a design Matrix Multiplier, from Matrix Multiply: grids multiplied, keys compared with queries. Softmax, from Softmax: scores turned into weights. Linear Layer, from Linear Layer: a learned matrix, the workhorse of every model. Activation, from GELU: a nonlinear function on every number. Normalizer, from Layer Norm: vectors kept at a steady size. Attention Head, from Attention: multi-head attention in one machine. Feed-Forward Block, from Feed-Forward Block: widen, bend, project back. Transformer Block, from Transformer Block: a whole transformer layer.

title: Linear Layer
text: Linear Layer Multiplies every vector by a learned matrix and adds a learned bias. It works on the last size only: every position of every sequence goes through the same weights, separately. Shapes […×C_in] in, […×C_out] out, where C_out is the Outputs setting. Settings Outputs: V, or 4 to 256. 32 by default. End a model with a Linear Layer whose Outputs is V: those are the scores the Core wants. Bias: on by default. Parameters C_in × C_out, plus C_out for the bias. They start as PyTorch's do: uniform within ±1/√C_in, with the bias at zero. In PyTorch self.hidden = nn.Linear(C_in, C_out) h = self.hidden(x) Notes PyTorch stores the matrix the other way round, as [C_out × C_in]. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Linear Layer: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Matrix Multiplier
text: Matrix Multiplier Multiplies two grids of numbers, the main input on the left and the side input on the right. In attention it does two jobs: comparing every query with every key, with Transpose on, and mixing the values by the weights that come out of the softmax. Shapes […×n×k] and […×k×m] in, […×n×m] out. With Transpose on, the side input is […×m×k]. The sizes in front must match, or the side input can be a single [k×m] grid shared by all. Settings Transpose: off by default. Flips the side input's last two sizes before multiplying. Parameters None: both inputs come from other machines. In PyTorch scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) mixed = weights @ v Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Matrix Multiply: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Head Merger
text: Head Merger Joins the heads back into one vector per position: the reverse of the Head Splitter. Shapes [B×H×T×d] in, [B×T×(H·d)] out. Parameters None. In PyTorch def merge_heads(x): B, H, T, D = x.shape return x.transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, H * D) Notes Follow it with a Linear Layer to mix what the heads found: that is the output projection, W_O. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Feed-Forward Block
text: Feed-Forward Block Two Linear Layers with an Activation between them: widen each vector, bend it, project it back. It works on every position separately. Attention moves information between positions; this block processes it in place. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Expand: 1, 2 or 4. 4 by default. The hidden width is Expand × C. Function: ReLU, GELU or SiLU. GELU by default. Parameters 2 × E × C² + E × C + C, where E is Expand. In PyTorch self.ffn = FeedForward(C, 4 * C, gelu_tanh) x = x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x)) Notes With Expand at 4, it holds two thirds of a transformer layer's weights. Interpretability research suggests these layers store much of what a model knows about the world. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Feed-Forward Block: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Gate
text: Gate Multiplies its two inputs number by number, so one signal can scale, open or close another. Shapes The same shapes as the Residual Junction takes. Parameters None. In PyTorch y = F.silu(self.gate(x)) * self.up(x) Notes Gates sit inside the feed-forward layers of most recent language models. SwiGLU multiplies SiLU(xW₁) by a second projection xW₃ before projecting back down. To build one: two Linear Layers reading the same input, an Activation set to SiLU after one of them, a Gate joining them, and a Linear Layer back to the original width. LSTMs, the recurrent networks that came before transformers, controlled their memory with gates like this. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Normalizer
text: Normalizer Rescales each vector to a steady size, then applies a learned gain and, for LayerNorm, a learned offset. Shapes […×C] in, the same shape out. Each vector is normalized over its last size. Settings Kind: LayerNorm by default, or RMSNorm, which skips the mean and the offset. LLaMA uses RMSNorm. Parameters 2 × C for LayerNorm, C for RMSNorm. ε is 1e-5. In PyTorch self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(C) h = self.norm1(x) Notes Put one at the start of each branch, before attention or the feed-forward block, and one before the final Linear Layer. This pre-norm layout is GPT-2's, and nearly every model since uses it. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Layer Norm: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Position Table
text: Position Table A learned vector for every position in the context, from 0 to T − 1. It takes no input. Add its output to the token vectors with a Residual Junction, and every position carries both what it is and where it is. Shapes No input. [T×C] out, which a Residual Junction adds to every sequence in the batch. Settings Width: 4 to 256. 32 by default. Match it to the Embedding Table's width. Parameters T × C, where T is the context length, 64. In PyTorch self.pos = nn.Embedding(T, C) x = self.embed(tokens) + self.pos(torch.arange(T)) Notes Learned positions are what GPT-2 used. Most recent models instead rotate each query and key by an angle that depends on its position (RoPE), so that attention scores depend on how far apart two tokens are. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Scaler
text: Scaler Multiplies everything by a constant. Shapes Any shape in, the same shape out. Settings Factor: 1/√d by default, where d is the last size of the input. Also 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 2 and 4. Parameters None. In PyTorch q = q / math.sqrt(d) Notes In attention it does not matter much where the 1/√d goes: scaling the queries or scaling the scores gives the same result. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Delay Line
text: Delay Line Shifts a sequence later in time: position t receives what position t − k had, and the first k positions receive zeros. It lets a position see a fixed number of steps back. Shapes A sequence […×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Steps: 1 to 4. 1 by default. Parameters None. In PyTorch def delay(x, steps): return F.pad(x, (0, 0, steps, 0))[..., : x.shape[-2], :] prev = delay(e, 1) Notes Attention can look back any distance, so transformers rarely need a fixed delay. Some architectures keep one anyway: RWKV mixes every token with the one before it, a learned blend called token shift. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Softmax
text: Softmax Turns each row of scores into weights that are positive and sum to one, along the last size. Shapes Any shape in, the same shape out. Parameters None. In PyTorch weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1) Notes Don't end a model with one. The Core applies its own softmax to the scores it receives, as PyTorch's cross-entropy loss does, and a second one squashes them so flat that the model can never be confident. In an attention build, the Softmax's output picture is the attention pattern: one row per position. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Softmax: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Head Splitter
text: Head Splitter Cuts each vector into H equal parts and gives the heads a dimension of their own, so the machines after it work on every head at once. Shapes [B×T×C] in, [B×H×T×(C/H)] out. Settings Heads: 1, 2, 4 or 8. 4 by default. Parameters None. In PyTorch def split_heads(x, heads): B, T, C = x.shape return x.view(B, T, heads, C // heads).transpose(1, 2) Notes With a Head Splitter and a Head Merger you can build multi-head attention from parts: split the queries, keys and values the same way, and the Matrix Multipliers, Scaler, Causal Mask and Softmax all work on every head in parallel. Making it The Fabricator makes it with no mask. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Transformer Block
text: Transformer Block One whole transformer layer in one machine: normalize, attend, add back; normalize, feed forward, add back. Stack them to make a GPT. Shapes A sequence [B×T×C] in, the same shape out. Settings Heads: 1, 2, 4 or 8. 4 by default. Expand: 1, 2 or 4. 4 by default. Function: ReLU, GELU or SiLU. GELU by default. Parameters 12 × C² + 9 × C with Expand at 4: about 50,000 at width 64. In PyTorch self.block1 = Block(C, heads=4, hidden=4 * C, act=gelu_tanh) x = self.block1(x) Notes Its picture shows the attention pattern of its first head, like the Attention Head's. Making it The Fabricator makes it from a photomask of Transformer Block: verify the spec on a Bench, or find a salvaged mask in the ruins, which makes it unfused. See The Bench and the Fabricator.

title: Milestones
text: Milestones Every milestone is an advancement, in the frame the advancement screen gives it, and the frame lights up once you have made it. They run roughly in the order a world unfolds, though most chapters can be taken in any order. A first model Checkpoint Save a trained model. Cable an Embedding Table to a Model Core, train it on the Forecast Dataset and save it: Getting Started. What Comes Next Save a model that passes the Forecasting test. Saving tests a model on every benchmark; a first model passes this one once it has practised long enough. A Watched Pot Place a Forecaster by your furnaces or crops. It writes down what the furnaces and crops around it do: The Forecaster. Ahead of Time Have a Forecaster run your furnaces or crops ahead with a model it trusts. A model that passes Forecasting is trusted with machines once they have made about a dozen items; your own field may take a model trained on the Forecaster's own log. Further Ahead Have Forecaster II run blocks eight times as fast. The Fabricator makes Forecaster II from a transformer photomask; a model within 5% of its blocks runs them eight times as fast: The Forecaster. Borrowed Time Run a block ahead with an Hourglass bound to a Forecaster. The Fabricator makes it from an attention photomask, and it keeps time while carried. Sneak-use a Forecaster that runs blocks ahead to bind it, then use it on one of those blocks: The Forecaster. Agent Make an agent. Craft one and place it where it should live: Agents. Hello, World Give an agent a program of your own. Type one in its screen, or click it together from the palette. Storage Somewhere to Put It Make a Storage Drive. It keeps any number of kinds: Storage. Everything in One Place Place a Storage Terminal. Link it to a Drive Rack with Storage Links. Hands Off Place a Port, which moves items between the network and an inventory. Hold its front against a chest or a machine, and link its back to the network. Made to Order Have an Assembler craft for your network. Draw a recipe in an Assembler's grid and tell it how many to keep. Just Ask Have your network make something you asked for at a Storage Terminal. Click something the network can make in a Storage Terminal, ask for an amount and start it: Storage. The old world Ruins Find a ruin of the people who were here before. The old world's places stand far apart, each in the land that suits it: Ruins. Lost Words Dig an archive shard out of a ruin. Each is a piece of one record, with some of its text lost: The Archive. Bearings Tune a Wayfinder to a ruin a shard told you of. Use a Wayfinder and choose a kind of ruin; reading shards adds the places they write about: Ruins. The Archive Make an archive drive to file shards into. Shards of the same record filed together make one better copy. Restoration Place a Reader. It restores a record's lost text with a model of yours. Words, Not Letters Learn a vocabulary in a BPE Forge. A vocabulary learned from what you have recovered lets a model read words instead of letters: Tokens. It Reads Save a model that passes the Reading test. Train on an Archive Drive until the test loss is 1.40 or less: Models and Tests. Machines from scratch The Bench Place a Bench, where modules are wired from primitives. Each spec comes with cases that break the obvious design: The Bench and the Fabricator. Lithography Place a Fabricator, which makes machines from designs. Photomasks found in the ruins work in it too. Rows by Columns Verify a design for Matrix Multiply. The Layer Verify a design for the Linear Layer. It opens once matrix multiply is verified. Feed Forward Verify a design for the Feed-Forward Block. It opens once the linear layer is verified. On Average Verify a design for Mean. In Range Verify a layer norm that survives flat and far rows. It opens once mean is verified. A Smooth Bend Verify a design for GELU. Overflow Verify a softmax that survives large scores. Scores of a thousand overflow the obvious design. Paying Attention Verify a design for Attention. It opens once softmax is verified. The Block Verify a design for the Transformer Block. It opens once attention is verified. From Scratch Verify every spec on the Bench. Residual Lay a residual stream, the backbone every transformer is built around. Transformer layers read from it and add to it: The Residual Stream. Models that work Each benchmark is passed by saving a model that passes it; the table in Models and Tests says what to practise for each. A Place for Everything Save a model that passes the Recall test. Practise on the Storage Dataset. The Way Home Save a model that passes the Reversal test. Practise on the Errand Dataset. Once More From the Top Save a model that passes the Induction test. Practise on the Pattern Dataset; it takes two layers of attention. Pigeonholes Save a model that passes the Sorting test. Practise on the Sorting Dataset. Steady Hand Save a model that passes the Control test. Practise on the Process Dataset: the Core plays melts with the model's own choices, and it takes a model that attends to the whole melt. Prospector Save a model that passes the Survey test. Practise on the Survey Dataset; it takes attention that knows where each block stands in a row. Steady Wings Save a model that passes the Pilot test. Practise on the Flight Dataset: the Core flies the model's own flights, and it takes a model that reads the flight back to its start. Plain Words Save a model that passes the Orders test. Practise on the Orders Dataset; it takes a model too big to carry. A Whole Model Save one model that passes every test. A Model Core practises up to four kinds at once. Putting models to work At Your Service Place a Model Server. A bigger model stays in a server and answers over relays: Serving Models. Within Reach Place a relay. The plans turn up on relay masts and in vaults. Do What I Mean Have an agent carry out an order its model understood. Start a chat message with its name, such as Pip, bring me some bread. Its model has to have practised orders. Seen It Before Have an agent copy a build. Mark a build's corners and the block its copy stands on, and hand the marks to an agent whose model passes Induction: The Architect. Moving House Have an agent move a build, contents and all. The same marks, with move instead of copy. Strike Have a Surveyor find an ore with its model. The Fabricator makes a Surveyor from an attention photomask; give it a model that passes Survey: The Surveyor. Flight Lift Off Fly with a flight frame its pilot holds. Put a pilot that passes Pilot in a charged flight frame, wear it, and jump twice: Flight. Power Live Wire Place a Combustion Generator. It burns what a furnace burns: Power. Twice Over Smelt one ore into two ingots in a Smelter. The Fabricator makes a Smelter from a transformer photomask; give it power and raw ore. Salvage Salvage Find a salvaged model in a ruin. Each one failed in its own way: Salvaged Models. Answering Repair the field model that never answered. No Peeking Repair the field model that was never wrong. First and Last Repair the errand model that came home the wrong way. Steady Hands Repair the storeroom model that burned out. Shortcuts Repair the tall model that never learned to read.

title: Models and Tests
text: Models and Tests Every model is tested on ten benchmarks. Each test uses examples practice never shows, and each job asks its model in exactly the test's format, so a test score is how often an agent will decide right. Benchmark Practice The test Passes at Used for Forecasting Forecast Dataset crops' ages and machines' progress at every look loss ≤ 0.21 the Forecaster Recall Storage Dataset goods and their chests, then one kind asked again 90% storing Reversal Errand Dataset waymarks on the way out, then the way home 90% hauling Induction Pattern Dataset letters where a run comes round again 90% the Architect Sorting Sorting Dataset things named, and the kind of each, some made up 90% sorting Orders Orders Dataset orders, and what was meant by them 90% orders Reading Archive Drive records no shard carries loss ≤ 1.40 the Reader Control Process Dataset melts of each ore, held at 90% of their looks 90% the Smelter Survey Survey Dataset rows of ground, and where the first of an ore lies 90% the Surveyor Pilot Flight Dataset flights in each wind, held at 90% of their looks 90% the flight frame Hover over a benchmark on the Core's Tests tab for the exact format. The Try tab shows the model answering a fresh example, the way an agent would ask it. Practising several things The Core's four Data slots are practised together: every step draws its batch from one of them in turn. One model can learn everything, if it is big enough and shaped for it. Each benchmark asks for something different: forecasting a machine only needs the look just before, and so does forecasting an average field; recall has to find a pair far back; reversal needs to know where each waymark was; induction has to look back for what followed the same letter last time; sorting has to find the word in a name that settles its kind. Practising by playing Control is practised by playing, not from examples: the Core plays melts with the model's own choices, and the model learns from each choice by how much better the melt did after it than after other choices made at the same look and temperature. A choice that went well is learned from more, one that went badly less. It takes longer than learning from examples, since every step plays its melts first. A melt is held when 90% of its looks end in the band, which is what earns a Smelter's third ingot, and the test scores the share held of the ore the model holds worst. Holding a melt means foreseeing what comes, when the fresh charges drop the melt and how the ore drifts, which needs a model that knows where in the melt it is and which ore it began with. A model that sees only the last few characters holds most copper melts but no gold or iron; a two-block transformer passes after two to four hundred steps, though its score still swings now and then as it practises. Checkpoints Crafting A Checkpoint holds one model: its machines, its weights, how long it trained and its scores. Saving runs every test first, so the scores on a checkpoint are always the ones it earned. Saving over a checkpoint replaces the model on it. How big a model may be An agent can carry a model of up to 40,000 parameters in its head. A bigger model stays in a Model Server and is asked over relays: see Serving Models. The Train tab counts a model's parameters. Reading ahead A model that can see the letter it is asked to predict is not predicting anything. The Core checks every model for this. A model that reads ahead scores very well and means nothing; its checkpoint says so, and the Reader turns it away.

title: Power
text: Power Power moves in Forge Energy (FE) along Power Cables: from the blocks that make it to the blocks that store or use it, and to any other mod's block that takes FE. Making it The Combustion Generator burns what a furnace burns and makes 80 FE a tick while it burns. A fuel lasts half as long as in a furnace, so a coal makes 64,000 FE. It burns only while it has room for what it makes, and holds 32,000 FE of its own. Crafting Moving and storing it Power Cables join generators, cells and machines into one network. Each tick the machines take what they need from the generators, then from the cells; whatever the generators make beyond that charges the cells. An Energy Cell holds 1,000,000 FE and moves up to 2,000 FE a tick each way. Its faces fill in quarters as it charges, and a comparator beside it reads how full it is. Crafting Crafting The Smelter The Smelter smelts anything a furnace does on 80 FE a tick instead of fuel, an item every five seconds. From an ore or a raw ore it makes two of what a furnace makes from one. The Fabricator makes it from a transformer photomask. The controller Put a model in the Smelter's Controller slot, and each ore becomes a melt it holds in its band: at a look every four ticks it asks the model whether to cool the melt, hold it or heat it, and waits for the answer. A melt held in the band at 90% of its looks or more makes three ingots instead of two; a model passes the Control test by holding nine melts in ten of every ore the test plays. The slot is in the panel beside the Smelter's screen; between its ore and its ingots, the screen draws the melt look by look, the band shaded, and pointing at it tells how much of the last melt was held. A model learns this on the Process Dataset: see Models and Tests. Other blocks Hoppers and Ports feed the generator and the Smelter from any side and take the Smelter's ingots out. Other mods' cables can draw power from generators and cells, and give it to cells and the Smelter.

title: Ruins
text: Ruins The people who lived here before left their places behind: towers along the old roads, farms on the ridges, houses on the marshes, slips on the shores, and stranger halls. Every kind of ruin is rare, some rarer than others, and each stands only in the land that suits it, where the ground is near level: it takes travel to come across one, and a Wayfinder to find one on purpose. Places of a kind were built a few different ways, and the years have worn each its own way. Finding them A Wayfinder leads to ruins the archive has told you of. Use it to choose a kind to look for: it lists the relay towers, which everyone knows of, and every kind a shard you have read tells of; read a shard, by using it, and the places it writes about join the list. Its needle spins while it looks, longer the farther the nearest one lies, then points to the nearest ruin of that kind within 10,000 blocks; while you hold it, it says how far that is. Crafting Relay towers Stone towers, the tallest thing for half a day's walk: a base buttressed at the corners, the shaft set back above it and banded at each floor, and three rooms one over another, the store, the kitchen with its stove and the keeper's room, with a ladder up the north wall. At the top a walk on corbels, railed, with the bell that calls for coal, goes round the lamp room of glass in a copper frame, its great lamp of glass and redstone under a flared roof of copper gone green. At the tower's foot stands the relay house: stone below and a spruce frame above, the keeper's desk with the tower book on its lectern, and the stand where a big mind stood, ringed by accelerators in their cooling water. Some towers have lost their tops. In grassland, forest, taiga, snow and hills, at most one in each region 48 chunks across. Waymarks Stone pillars on stepped bases by stretches of the old road, a figure cut in the middle stone, a torch on top, little stones left at the foot and an arrow to the nearest inn; the ring where walkers made their fire, with a bench and a trough. Some pillars have fallen into the grass; one in six stands under a little roof with notes left on it. The commonest ruin: at most one in each region 24 chunks across. Three Wells A market town's square where two roads cross like an X: paving round three wells under their little roofs, a lamp at every corner, the bell at the crossing, the notice board with the market rules, stalls under wool awnings, benches under two trees, the bakery with its oven built out on the side, the school house by the east well with its painted door and its bell on the roof, and a stretch of the town wall. On plains, meadows and savannas, the rarest of the towns' ruins: at most one in each region 80 chunks across. Inns The inns of the Long Road, a day apart, the Halfway Inn and the Brown Hen: a timber frame on a stone footing (the Brown Hen's ground floor all stone), the upper floor jutting over the road on corbels, shuttered windows, two dormers and the chimney stack up the gable. Inside, the hearth still burns; the boards hang by the fire, the book lies behind the counter next to a pie, and the beds wait upstairs; a woodshed stands at the back, the stable across the yard with its roof part fallen, and the inn's sign by the road. At most one in each region 64 chunks across. Windmill farms The farms of the ridges: a windmill with a stone base and a boarded body, a railed stage round it and its tally board by the door, the barn with its hayloft and hoist, the pig pen and the hen house, a well in the yard, and three fields, wheat, beetroot, and potatoes and carrots, each with its ditch, its hedge and its scarecrow or hives. On plains, meadows, savannas and windswept hills, at most one in each region 56 chunks across. Watermills The mills of the orchard country, of birch and glass on a stone footing at the edge of a pond: the wheel out over the water on its axle, the millstone under its hopper inside, a race of stone beside it with the sluice nobody may open and a footbridge with a loose plank, the notices on the gate, a bench on the far side, old apple trees and hives among the flowers. Only by water deep enough, the wheel toward it: at most one in each region 56 chunks across. Stilt houses Houses of mud brick on decks over the marsh, their stilts down to the marsh floor, a boardwalk to the bank. A healer's house keeps its high shelves of labeled jars, the remedies on the bench, beds for the sick and her day book; a boat house keeps the day's catch and the tally on its wall. In swamps and mangrove swamps, at most one in each region 48 chunks across. Slipways A buttressed stone quay with steps down to the water, the shipwright's shed with its window for mending nets, the wood store and the fish market's price board; running out over the sea on posts, the frame of a ship never finished with a crane leaning over it, and beside it a ramp of stone into the water. Some frames are a big ship's, three times as long as any boat. Only where a beach or a stony shore meets deep enough water, the slip toward the sea: at most one in each region 40 chunks across. Tutor houses Halls of tuff between pillars, two tiers of tall windows under a cornice of copper, a relay on the roof, where minds were drilled and tested. Apprentices still stand in their row before the tutor's Bench; the teaching room keeps its tray of crystals, each on its card, in the light of its bay window; the apprentice hall across the yard keeps its dry box; and the drill yard, ringed with torches, has its boards drawn as small fields. In grassland, forest, taiga, savanna and cherry groves, at most one in each region 72 chunks across. The Archive at Vell Where everything was kept, dug into its hill. Its front faces the town: pillars of tuff, the portal under the first keepers' words, a broad flight of steps, the copying room's big window and the reading room's, where a lamp still burns on the long table; behind the front everything is under turf, and light wells of glass come up through the grass. A great stair goes down into the hill to the front hall and the finding book, the halls of shelves under their light wells, a stack sealed with clay, and the deepest room, where the oldest record is kept. At most one in each region 160 chunks across. The Deep Works A great mine in the hills. At the shaft head stand the headframe and its wheel, the board where miners wrote their names and rubbed them out coming up, the tool store and the sorting bins. A ladder goes down the shaft past a level of copper, a level of iron and coal with an amethyst hollow behind a door, and the deep stone, where an old tunnel was walled up; at the ninth level the gate is locked, and an old side door above it leads down another way. In windswept hills, meadows and savanna plateaus, at most one in each region 128 chunks across. Fallen relay masts Where a relay mast fell it broke a bowl in the ground, grassed over at the rim. The mast lies across it in three pieces of green copper, its relay half buried at the far end, stone thrown up round it; along the rim the keepers put a rope of chain on posts, and their sign. Its drive housing split open: the chest inside holds Archive Drives already filled with the relays' writing. At most one in each region 40 chunks across. Sealed stacks Deep under the ground, with no way in but a wall of clay: a vaulted hall of the archive sealed in its last days, its shelves in bays behind folded doors with wax over them, boxes of records in waxed cloth down the middle, the sealing book on its lectern, and a lamp left on the long table; roots have come down through the vault. Their boxes hold filled Archive Drives. At most one in each region 64 chunks across. Archive houses, relay masts and buried vaults Small houses of calcite between pillars of tuff under roofs of deepslate tiles, one corner usually fallen in, that kept records; open masts of green copper on stepped tuff footings, an old relay still on top of most of them; and, under a lantern on a post beside a hatch, deep rooms with a bank of old accelerators and two chests, every one holding a salvaged model. At most one in each region 56 chunks across, the vaults 64. What they hold Archive Shard: pieces of the archive, mostly of what was written about the place they lie in: a relay tower's shards are mostly its keepers' writing. See The Archive. Photomasks with salvaged designs: the Fabricator makes working but unfused machines from them, without a Bench. Linear layer, softmax and GELU masks turn up in houses, matrix multiply ones under the gravel, and attention, layer norm, feed-forward and transformer masks in vaults. See The Bench and the Fabricator. Schematic: Relays: the plans for relays, a pattern to copy that stays in the crafting grid. In relay towers, on masts and in vaults. What each place kept: coal and food in the towers, flour and seed on the farms, remedies in the marsh, timber and tools at the slips; Weight Crystal, blank Checkpoints and a little gold. Salvaged Model: see Salvaged Models.

title: Salvaged Models
text: Salvaged Models Every buried vault holds a Salvaged Model: the record of a model the old world built and could not make work. It keeps the model's machines, what it practised on and how it was trained. Each failed the way models often do. Rebuilding Put a salvaged model in a Model Core's Data slot and press Rebuild on the Data tab. Its machines are built in front of the Core as they were found: they need clear space, and they drop nothing when broken. Its training settings come with it. Train it as it is first, and watch how it fails. The loss curve, the Inspect tab and the machines themselves all have something to say. Repairing Find what is wrong and put it right: change a machine's settings, add or replace a machine, or change how it trains. A salvaged model has a budget of 1,500 steps per run to reach its goal; when a run runs out, Reset its weights and try again. A repaired model is worth experience, and what it took to repair it is worth more.

title: Shapes
text: Shapes Every value in a model is a grid of numbers, a tensor, and its shape says how big each side of the grid is. The Model Core checks every shape before it trains anything, the same way PyTorch would fail on the first batch, but with a clearer message. Reading a shape Shapes are written outermost first: [B×T×32] is a batch of B sequences, each T positions long, with 32 numbers at every position. Letter Means B Batch: how many sequences are processed at once. Set on the Core. T Time: positions in a sequence, up to the context length of 64. Every other number is a size you chose, like the 32 above, or the vocabulary size V, which shows as its value: 78, one for each letter, digit and mark a model knows, and the line break, or more with a tokenizer. The last dimension is the one machines work on: a Linear Layer turns [B×T×32] into [B×T×64] by mixing the 32 numbers at each position into 64 new ones, the same way at every position. A shape with fewer dimensions stretches to fit, as in PyTorch: the Position Table's [T×32] adds onto every sequence of a [B×T×32] batch. What the Core expects The Core sends out token ids, shaped [B×T], and wants back one score for every possible next token at every position: [B×T×V]. Whatever happens in between is up to you. When shapes disagree Press Check on the Core, or look at a machine. A machine whose inputs don't fit says what it got and what it needs. Common causes: A Residual Junction or Gate whose two inputs have different widths. A Matrix Multiplier whose inner sizes don't match. With Transpose on, it multiplies by the side input turned on its side, which is what comparing queries with keys needs. The last machine before the Core not ending in V. Shapes flow forward, so fix the earliest problem first: a wrong width early on makes every later machine look wrong too. The Inspect tab on the Core lists every machine in the order data reaches it. In PyTorch Shape errors are the most common bug in real model code. PyTorch only finds them when the code runs; reading shapes the way the Core does, before running anything, is a habit worth taking with you.

title: Storage
text: Storage Storage Drives in a Drive Rack, joined by Storage Links to a Storage Terminal and to Ports, make one storage network. It keeps any number of kinds of item, finds any of them from the terminal, and moves them in and out of chests and machines on its own. Nothing in it needs power, and nothing switches off. Drives and racks A Storage Drive holds 262,144 items, of as many kinds as you like: a kind costs nothing but its items. What a drive holds goes with it, so a drive moved to another rack takes everything with it, and its tooltip says how full it is. Crafting Crafting A Drive Rack holds eight drives. Beside each bay a light shows how full its drive is: dim while it is empty, teal while it has room, amber once it is three quarters full, red when it is full. Links Storage Links join racks, terminals and Ports into one network. Every storage block that touches another joins it, on any face, except a Port's front. There are no channels and no limit on how many blocks a network joins. Storage Links are not the signal cables models are wired with: the two never connect. Crafting The Storage Terminal Crafting The terminal shows everything its network keeps, with how many of each kind, and lights up once its network has somewhere to keep things. Click a kind to take a stack, right-click to take half, shift-click to move a stack into your inventory. Click the grid with a stack to put it in, right-click to put in one. Shift-click a stack in your inventory to put it away. The button beside the search box sorts by name (Az), by how many (#) or by mod (@); shift-click it to reverse. The search box finds things by name, every word at once. Other facts take a sign before them: Search Finds ingot names holding "ingot" @minecraft things from that mod #ingots things with a tag holding "ingots" $hunger tooltips holding "hunger" *copper ids holding "copper" -iron everything except what holds "iron" iron | gold either one (log | planks) -oak groups >64, <10, =1, >=1k how many are kept (k for thousands, m for millions) @minecraft ingot -iron finds every ingot but iron, and >1k everything there are more than a thousand of. Ports A Port holds its front against an inventory (a chest, a barrel, a furnace or any other machine) and moves items between it and the network, 64 items a tick: 1,280 a second. Placed against a block, it faces that block; sneak-use one of its faces to turn its front there. Its sides show what it does, and light while it moves things. Crafting Import takes everything from the inventory into the network; with a filter, only those kinds. Under a furnace it takes the furnace's output. Export puts the kinds its filter names into the inventory, as long as the network has them and the inventory has room. Stock keeps the inventory holding a set number of each kind its filter names: it tops each one up from the network, and takes any extra back. Window opens the inventory to the network, which keeps items there and takes them out as if it were a drive. A window with a higher priority is filled first, and a filter limits what may go in. To set the filter, click one of its slots with a stack, or shift-click the stack in your inventory; click a slot empty-handed to clear it. The screen says how many items the Port moved in the last second. A Port can also filter by what things are. Put a filter model in the slot beside its screen: a Checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server, whose model passes Sorting (Models and Tests). Then a filter slot holding something renamed Food, Plants, Wood, Stone, Ores or Tools stands for that whole kind: importing, the Port takes every thing the model says is of it; exporting, it hands out every such thing the network holds. The model is asked about each thing once, by name, as the sorting test asks; a thing it is not sure of counts as other. Stocking keeps to things, not kinds. Assemblers An Assembler on the network crafts one recipe from what the network keeps, and puts the result back. Draw the recipe in its grid the way you would on a crafting table: click a cell with a stack to put that kind there, or empty-handed to clear it. The grid holds pictures, not items. What the recipe makes shows beside it, and the Assembler waits while its screen is open, so a recipe half drawn never crafts. Tell it how many of the result to keep. Whenever the network holds fewer, it crafts, up to four crafts a tick, as long as the network has the ingredients; whatever a recipe leaves behind, such as an empty bucket, goes back into the network. One Assembler can keep another stocked: one that keeps sticks lets one that makes torches go on as long as there is coal. Crafting Asking for things What the network's Assemblers can make shows in the terminal too: with Craft in place of a count when there is none of it, and with a teal corner when there is. Click it, or middle-click or Ctrl-click one there is some of, to ask for an amount. The terminal plans it as you type: a tree of everything it takes, each step with how many come from storage, how many crafts make the rest (×) and how many are missing (−). Start it, and the network's Assemblers work through the plan, any number of jobs at once; Assemblers drawing the same recipe share its crafts. What a job makes along the way it keeps to itself until it is done, so nothing else takes it first. A job may start with something missing: it waits, and goes on as soon as what it lacks reaches the network. When it is done, everything it made goes into the network, and you hear so wherever you are. Jobs, beside the search box, lists the jobs running on the network, how far each has got and what it waits for; × stops one, and what it has made so far goes back into the network.

title: The Residual Stream
text: The Residual Stream A transformer is built around a running sum. The embedding starts it; every layer reads it, computes something, and adds its result back; the last layer turns the sum into scores. That running sum is the residual stream. A Residual Stream is a conduit for it. Crafting How it flows Each block passes the stream on out of its front. The chevrons on its sides point the way. An output touching a stream block, face to face or through a cable, adds into the stream at that block. An input touching a stream block reads the stream as it arrives there, before that block's additions. An input at the front of the last block reads the whole sum. A stream starts out empty: the first thing added to it, usually the embedding, is what it carries from there on. A stream placed against the front of another one carries on from it, and one placed against an output starts there. Sneak-use a face to turn a block. A layer on the stream This is one transformer layer, laid out the way it is usually drawn: read, normalize, compute, add back. Stack more layers by making the stream longer. The Transformer Block does all of this inside one block, residual additions included, so it goes on a line of its own, not on a stream: there it would add the stream to itself twice. Why a stream Each layer refines the sum rather than replacing it, so a layer that has nothing useful to add yet can leave it alone. Training sees the same shortcut: the gradient flows back along the stream to every layer directly. In a plain stack of layers it has to pass through every layer on the way down, and in a deep one it fades before it reaches the bottom.
