You can watch it happen: the amber wave that runs back while a model trains reaches every layer on a stream as bright as it started, and dims layer by layer down a deep plain stack. Rules Two streams can't flow into one block, and a stream can't run in a circle. A machine reads the stream where its input touches it and adds where its output does. Reading after the place it adds back would make a loop. A cable touching a stream and nothing else that drives it carries the stream. A cable touching two streams and no output carries neither: hold a Tensor Probe to see what a cable carries.

title: The Surveyor
text: The Surveyor The Surveyor finds the ores in the ground around it, and the old world's caches: chests and barrels it filled that nobody has opened since. It reads the ground a row of sixteen blocks at a time, a letter for each block, and asks its model where the first of each ore or cache in the row lies, just as the Survey test does. Every answer is checked against the block: a right one is kept, and the row is asked again for the next of that kind; a wrong one leaves that kind unfound until the next survey. How it reads the ground Its model is a language model, so the ground reaches it as text: each block a letter, a row of sixteen blocks sixteen letters. Ground: S stone, D deepslate, T other rock, A air, W water, L lava, B bedrock. Ores: C coal, I iron, U copper, O gold, R redstone, Z lapis, X diamond, E emerald; and K, a cache. After the row come >, the kind asked for and :, and the model answers with the first such block's place, a to p, or - for none: SSSTTIIDDDDSSSSS>I:f. Surveying Put a model in the Surveyor's Model slot, in the panel beside its screen: a Checkpoint, or a Relay Card tuned to a Model Server. It surveys 16 blocks each way and from 15 above it to 48 below: 4,096 rows, 32 read a tick and 64 questions put to the model at once. Then it starts over, so what is mined drops out of the next survey. Its screen shows the eight ores and caches, three by three, with how many of each it found; along the screen's foot, how far the survey has gone. Hold a Survey Rod within 48 blocks of it to see what it found through the ground, a box in each ore's colour and caches in violet. Digging for it An agent's mine goes to what a Surveyor within 48 blocks found when nothing of the kind lies within its own reach of 8, and digs its way to anything buried: down where the ore lies at least as far below as aside, otherwise along the longer way, two blocks high. It tunnels only through rock and earth, never through a machine, a container or anything an axe would cut, and goes round such a block the other way when it can; it gives up a tunnel that would let in water or lava, or that finds no way round. To mine iron is to mine iron ore: repeat (mine 8 iron, put) digs where the iron is and brings it home. mine caches digs to a cache and takes what it holds. Agents mining near each other work as a crew: each takes a block no other has picked, so a crew spreads over what a Surveyor found instead of crowding the nearest ore. Its model A model learns this on the Survey Dataset, and passes the Survey test by answering 90% of its questions right: see Models and Tests. Finding the first of a letter takes looking back over the row and knowing where each block stands in it. A model that sees only the last few characters, or a single layer of attention without positions, stays near half; a two-block transformer passes after about 1,000 steps. A model that reads ahead finds nothing, so the Surveyor refuses it.

title: Tokens
text: Tokens A model never sees text, only tokens: numbers that each stand for a piece of text. Without a tokenizer, every character is a token, 78 in all: the letters, digits and marks, the space and the line break. Reading by the character is simple but short-sighted. Every word costs several predictions, and the 64 tokens a model reads at once cover only 64 characters. The BPE Forge The BPE Forge learns a vocabulary from the text on an Archive Drive by byte-pair encoding: Start with the characters. Count every pair of neighbouring tokens in the text. Join the most frequent pair into one new token, everywhere it occurs. Repeat until the vocabulary is as big as you asked. So t and h become th, th and e become the, and a space and the become ␣the. Common words end up as single tokens and rare ones stay in pieces, so any text can still be written. Merges stay inside a word: a word keeps the space before it, every digit stands alone, and punctuation keeps to itself. Crafting Put in a drive and a Tokenizer, pick a size, and watch the drive's text fall into fewer, longer tokens. Every merge is written onto the tokenizer as soon as it is learned, so you can take it out at any time. The forge carries on from the merges a tokenizer already has. A bigger size keeps every token of a smaller one, and a smaller size cuts a tokenizer back to the vocabulary it was on its way through. Crafting (Shapeless) Using a tokenizer Put the tokenizer in the Model Core's Tokenizer slot, and models built there read and write its tokens. Archive text in the data slots is cut into them, and so is whatever you say to the model through a Terminal. Datasets and the orders agents are given are always spelled out one character at a time, which every vocabulary can do. The tokenizer sets V: the rows of the embedding's table and the scores the last layer gives. Changing it reshapes those layers, so they start over. A saved model keeps the tokenizer it was trained with. What size? Longer tokens see further. At 512 tokens, a token of archive text carries about two and a half characters, so 64 tokens reach back about 160 characters instead of 64. More tokens cost weights. The embedding has a row and the last layer a score for every token: V × width weights each. Rare tokens learn slowly. A token seen only a few times in practice has little to learn from. Losses are counted per character, not per token, so models with different tokenizers compare fairly: a token's loss is shared among the characters it stands for.

title: Training
text: Training Training repeats one step thousands of times: run the model on a batch of text, measure how wrong it was, work out which way every weight should move to be less wrong, and move them a little. The loss A language model scores every possible next token. Softmax turns those scores into probabilities: The loss is the cross-entropy: the average, over every position, of how surprised the model was by the token that actually came next. A model that knows nothing spreads its bets evenly over all V tokens, and so starts near Every curve starts there. A loss of 0 would mean certainty about every next token, which no honest model reaches on real text. Losses are counted per character: a token's loss is shared among the characters it stands for, so a model that reads with a tokenizer compares fairly with one that reads by the character. For datasets, where only some positions have a right answer, the Core also measures accuracy: how often the top-scoring token is the right one. Practice and test The training loss is measured on the batches the model practises on, averaged over recent steps. The test loss is measured on examples practice never shows. When the two part ways, with training loss still falling while the test loss stalls or rises, the model is memorising its practice instead of learning what generalises. Models are judged on their tests alone. The settings Learning rate (LR). How far each step moves the weights. Too small and nothing happens for a long time; too large and the loss jumps around or explodes. The Core trains with AdamW, the optimizer most language models use. It scales each weight's step by the size of its recent gradients, so the learning rate sets the step size fairly directly: with the usual β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999 and weight decay λ = 0.01 on weight matrices. The first 20 steps warm up from zero to the full learning rate. Batch. How many sequences each step looks at. Bigger batches give a steadier gradient but cost more per step. Clip. Gradient clipping caps the size of the whole gradient before the step: It rescues the occasional huge gradient without changing ordinary steps. It does not rescue a learning rate that is too large on every step. Speed. Watch trains slowly enough to follow the curve; Max trains as fast as the Core can. Reading the curve Flat at the start, then a sudden drop: the model found a mechanism. Attention models often do this. Falling, then flattening above the goal: the model has learned all it can see. Give it more to work with: more context, more width, more layers. Jagged and climbing: the steps are too big. Lower the learning rate. Both losses suspiciously low: something lets the model see the answer. The Core flags a model that reads ahead. Watching it learn While a model trains, waves run through its blocks every two seconds. A teal pulse travels from the tokens to the loss, lighting each machine as the batch reaches it, as brightly as the values it puts out. Then an amber pulse runs back from the loss, lighting each machine as brightly as the gradient that reaches it. A machine that stays dark on the way back hardly learns: almost no gradient reaches it. Above each machine floats its output for one example of practice: a bar per entry for a vector, a cell per entry for a matrix, amber above zero and blue below. An attention head shows its pattern instead, which earlier tokens each token looks at. Look at a hologram to read the value under your crosshair. Hold a Tensor Probe to see the holograms when nothing is training. When training stops Training stops when you press Stop or when a machine of the model changes. It also stops when the loss diverges: if it turns into NaN, or climbs far above where it started. A salvaged model adds a budget: a limited number of steps per run, after which you reset the weights and try again. Reset throws the learned weights away so the next run starts fresh. Check reads the model again and reports any problem without training.

title: Machines and Cables
text: Machines and Cables A model is a graph of operations, and you build that graph out of blocks. Values flow out of one machine and into the next through cables, from the Model Core's tokens to the scores it takes back. Ports Every machine computes one output from its inputs, and each face of the block has a job: Front: the output. Back: the main input. Every other face: the side input, on machines that take two inputs, such as the Residual Junction or the Matrix Multiplier. One-input machines leave their sides unused, and the Position Table has no input at all. The Model Core sends tokens out of its front and takes the finished scores in through any other face. Look at a machine to see which port the face under your crosshair is. A machine placed against another machine's output takes that output as its input; placed against an input, it feeds it; placed against a cable or a residual stream, it reads it. Anywhere else its output points away from you. Sneak-use a face to turn the output to that face; sneak-using the output face itself turns the machine around. Networks Cables that touch form a network, and a network carries exactly one value. So every network needs exactly one source, a machine's front or the Core's front, and any number of inputs may read it. Two sources on one network is an error, and so is an input on a network with no source. Colors Colored cables only join cables of their own color, while plain cables join any color. That lets two networks run side by side without mixing. Dye eight cables at a time; a water bucket washes the color out again. Crafting Crafting Tracing a value With a Tensor Probe in hand, looking at a cable tells you which machine drives it and how many inputs read it. Use the probe on a cable to list every port on its network in chat. The probe also shows every machine's output as a hologram above it, from the last time the model ran: look at one to read its values. See Training for what they show while a model learns.
